title: Check yourself: when accessors are worth writing

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: What does this page say about the run-time cost of a trivial getter in frequently executed code?

options.text: It costs about as much as reading the field, once the JIT inlines it
options.says: Pitfall 4: the JIT compiler inlines trivial getters and setters, so they cost the same as direct field access in hot code.

options.text: It costs a method call each time, so hot loops should read the field
options.says: Pitfall 4 calls the overhead rarely a real concern, because the call is inlined away.

options.text: It costs a copy of the value each time, so objects should not be returned
options.says: A4 says returning a primitive or a reference costs the same; only a getter that builds a defensive copy pays for the copy.

origin.section: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

questions.stem: Which practice does this page's list of pitfalls caution against?

options.text: Naming a boolean field's getter isActive rather than getActive
options.says: Key point 4 gives is as the getter prefix for a boolean, so isActive follows the convention.

options.text: Checking every setter argument before assigning the field
options.says: The page says to always validate input in setters to maintain object integrity.

options.text: Generating a getter and a setter for each field by default
options.says: Pitfall 1: avoid creating getters and setters for all fields without considering their necessity.

origin.section: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

concepts: The JIT inlines trivial accessors, so they cost what a direct field access costs.
Getters and setters are not written for every field by default.
